utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I must apologise that a matter caused the Chamber to be delayed coming in. I'm sorry that we kept you waiting. Yes, Ms. Somers. May I remind you, Admiral, of the affirmation you took at the beginning of your evidence, which still applies. Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Admiral Jokic. I wanted to quickly return to a few points from yesterday's examination and ask you about Captain Kovacevic a little more. During the time period that the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade was subordinated to you, did Captain Kovacevic report to you or to General Strugar?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I just notify the transcript people that it reads 422. It should read 472nd. That's line 20. Are you aware of any exceptions where Captain Kovacevic reported to General Strugar and not to you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only say that he often went to the command post in Trebinje because the brigade was his superior unit and the brigade was located in the Trebinje area. Therefore, the communication between him, the brigade command, and the command of the 2nd Operational Group was quite assiduous. This was much closer for him to get to in terms of distance, and also in terms of, perhaps, his objectives.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: However, your command post was at Kupari; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In terms of military hierarchy, it would have been quite in order for him to report on a daily basis in the evening at about 5.00 in the afternoon as all other commanders used to come. However, on account of problems in his own battalion, he often reported that he was unable to -- to make it there because he was busy where he was. I would usually accept this, Chief of Staff or myself, whoever received the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: But he was to have reported to you in Kupari?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He often phoned.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you describe the relationship as you saw it between General Strugar and Captain Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning I was not aware of that naturally, but during the course of my command and later, I understood clearly that General Strugar was very fond of Captain Kovacevic and that he was impressed by him. This was a brave man, after all, held in high esteem, capable. He was even physically attractive as a soldier, as an officer. So he impressed everyone favourably. I don't know if they used to know each other earlier or not, but I understood clearly that he enjoyed all of the general's support and protection. There were one or two particular instances that I heard of this later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you aware of any gifts or special favours between Captain Kovacevic and General Strugar?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is something I heard later on in 1992 when the Dubrovnik operation was over. He was awarded a flat in Podgorica, skipping people who had been ahead of him on the waiting list, in return for which I believe he gave a passenger vehicle as a present.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you say he was awarded a flat, Admiral, to whom are you referring? Who is he?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean Captain Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Admiral, you mentioned earlier that Captain Kovacevic's objectives were closer to Trebinje. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I had in mind was that his command was located in the Trebinje area and he knew all those people there, at the command post of the 2nd Operational Group. He also had people who he cared about, and they cared about him, too. As for us sailors, to our command he was a new face; I'd never seen him before. Therefore, he spent more time with those people since they were part of his original command, and everything he had was there. He was only temporarily resubordinated to me, only for those specific operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Admiral. His obligation, however, was to report to you. That is correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By all means, which he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever he had to. It's just I'm saying that --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Admiral Jokic. I just want to clarify a point. You said that Captain Kovacevic was given a flat. Now, who gave him a flat?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Pavle Strugar was the commander of the 2nd army in Podgorica at the time, the army that had been set up in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And he gave -- you're saying that General Strugar gave him the flat?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what he told me. I heard that from him personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: From whom? From whom?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Captain Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And who gave Captain Kovacevic the vehicle? Who gave Captain Kovacevic the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He, Captain Kovacevic, gave the vehicle to General Strugar. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. How would you characterise your relationship with General Strugar?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a subordinate commander, I had a fair, correct relationship with him. We never clashed, not officially, in no way at all, and I think I was loyal to him in every way. We knew each other from before, not too well, but while I was the commander of the Boka sector and he was the commander of the Montenegrin Territorial Defence, we saw each other occasionally. There were no problems between us, no problems of official or personal nature. At least from my point of view, there were no problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Admiral. Did you have a sense that you were trusted or less than trusted by General Strugar? What was your perception?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as a commander he had trust, but he was very often dissatisfied with the general situation in terms of control and command, in terms of the results we were getting, in terms of daily problems throughout our units. Globally speaking, I think very often he was unhappy. I am sure that he was facing his own problems with the TO back in Podgorica. As concerns me specifically, I know of several examples where he was --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- when he was unhappy about the blockade from the sea, from where the sea was, because we did not have sufficient ships. We only had the two patrol boats patrolling the local line, so occasionally it would happen that Croatian boats at night would enter the town with arms, smuggled arms, on board. There were cases where the blockade had been broken through. He intervened, and he insisted that the blockade be preserved. He was absolutely right in requesting this. There were cases of indiscipline, of people getting wounded, of acts of provocation, and he always made his displeasure clear in these cases. There were several cases where people were wounded and killed at Bosanka, but I -- I expect that we shall deal with this later.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Admiral, do you know how General Strugar perceived you? Were you viewed as a tough commander? Were you -- what was -- if you know, what was the perception of you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't say. I can give you one example. We were at the command post. I had what was perhaps a bit of a sharp dialogue, a conversation with General Perisic, and he said he believed that General Perisic was right in that case and said he believed that General Perisic was the best commander he ever had. I was a bit crestfallen over that. I was disappointed by his position, because I believe that I, in fact, was right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Admiral, moving on, ask you about an incident involving the Budva Territorial Defence unit and a disciplinary issue over that. Do you recall such an incident where you took measures?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was about the Budva territorial company. It was a weak unit with poor discipline. They failed to carry out my orders, and once during an inspection I found several of them in some villages in Zupa. They were looting and trying to get away in a vehicle. I called their commander and ordered that they should leave the front line together with the whole unit. There had been several interventions that were made. I failed to give way, and the whole unit went back to Budva.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you send them back to Budva?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And did you retain the unit or did you disband the unit?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not the one who set up those territorial companies. Back then, we had a coordination body, a body that was in charge of coordination. Djurickovic, who was the Chief of Staff of the Territorial Defence staff of Montenegro, he was the coordinator for the territorial companies. He carried out coordination between those companies in the command of the 9th sector. We were unable to do that since those companies were quite many. Therefore, he was the one who set up those units, who mobilised those units and it was down to him really. He was the person in charge. I merely used those units pursuant to a joint plan that we agreed. There was a plan to use those units.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: At the time of your dealing with the disciplinary problem of the Budva territorial company, was it in the course of battle, and if so, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was outside of battle. That was during a lull in the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The -- an incident, if you recall, in an area called Cibaca in late 1991. Do you recall an incident involving indiscipline by soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. According to a plan that we had, we were supposed to send a unit on leave, as we said, after 45 days of continuous operations. Units in part or in whole would be sent on leave. They would be allowed to go back home. But I was not able to discipline that particular unit. I was not able to prevent them from using arms. So at first we tried to take the arms away from them. This was difficult to carry out, however, and it proved impossible eventually. I called General Strugar. I informed him I was unable to do that and I asked for his assistance. This was a unit of Montenegrins, and they were friendlier with a commander who was a Montenegrin himself. I didn't even speak their dialects. I asked him to speak to them. He accepted --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- he came there and the two of us together.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Who is -- when you say "him" --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Strugar.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the unit lined up with its commander and all the people who were there. The boss was there, too. He addressed them, he gave a speech the kind of speech that a commander would only be expected to give. He appealed to them to preserve discipline, to keep up a good level of discipline. He allowed them to keep their arms. They appealed to him to keep their arms and so that they wouldn't use it. Reluctantly he agreed to this. However, as soon as they boarded the buses the shooting began through the windows of the bus.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In your presence?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as they turned the bend.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And in the presence of General Strugar as well?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It was at a distance of about 500 metres from where we were standing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This bus that the shooting came from.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: These units were subordinate to General Strugar?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes the Territorial Defence units.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What did General Strugar do about it? What measures did he take at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't take any measures. He could not take any measures, because he had so many major problems he was facing at the time, this was just one of many problems that we faced.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What kind of firearms were they using? What kind of arms, excuse me, were involved in this incident of indiscipline?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by apology I object to the way that my learned friend and colleague is examining this witness. The admiral is answering questions that are asked. He wishes to provide an explanation of what he says, however, my colleague interrupts him with no obvious need and would not even allow him to finish his sentence. This is later on reflected in an illogical and inconsistent transcript. If a question is asked, can we please allow the admiral to please finish answering?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you could just carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. When the question is answered, I just try to move on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Admiral, my question to you was: What kind of arms were involved in this incident of indiscipline?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usual infantry weapons, automatic weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: To your knowledge --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: To your knowledge were any measures taken even at any time after the incident against these acts of indiscipline?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in relation to this specific incident or generally?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, in relation to this specific incident.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, there were a number of problems, major problems, continuing problems. We were simply overwhelmed by all these developments. This was a great blow to the authority of General Strugar. He was the most senior officer there, and this very much affected his military dignity and pride. Let me try to explain this. With Montenegrins it's very difficult to take weapons away from them and send them home without their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I very much appreciate your explanation. I think you've answered your question. Thank you very much. The various organs within which discipline is dealt in the military would include what particular bodies? If you can give a very brief overview.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of disciplinary infringements, the commanders, the unit commanders, would have been responsible, would have been in charge of that, each in terms of their respective rank and position. That's as far as infringements and violations are concerned. Major violations, there are always military courts. And as for criminal acts there are civilian courts. However there were major problems in the way all these institutions functioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask you to turn your attention to tab 11 of your binders, please. Admiral Jokic, before you is a document from the office of the military prosecutor, and it refers to the military court in Sarajevo for a violation or an indictment, rather, against an individual named Veselin Simovic, a reserve soldier who was, as it goes through, accused of killing civilians -- right, civilians in Kijev Do in Trebinje municipality on or about 13 November, 1991. He was a member of the 2nd Operational Group. Are you aware of how many or -- are you aware of the number of indictments such as this one which may have been issued during the time period where you were in the Dubrovnik theatre?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at least as I could see for myself by looking at the records of the military court in Podgorica or, rather, in Tivat, there were about 68 indictments for crimes, and there were over 150 criminal reports for robbery mostly. However, looking at the Sarajevo courts, I don't know about that. This was the biggest military court that we had, and it had jurisdiction over the territory in which the operation around Dubrovnik was taking place.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you undertake an inquiry as to investigations or prosecutions in connection with any particular preparation? Did you undertake -- did you look into the number of criminal prosecutions or cases that had been brought for any particular reason?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By all means. I was in part familiar with all of that, but I do have to say that at the beginning, in the period under discussion here, October, November, and December, this court, this military court in Tivat had only been set up, and we were just beginning to create the conditions for its work. Therefore, the proper functioning of this court began as late as December and perhaps as late as 1992, and that's when the cases began to be prosecuted. Most of those cases were in relation to looting and arson. There were several cases of people wounding each other through the use of weapons. However, looting and arson accounted for most of the cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did any of the cases you looked at deal with shelling for October, November, or December of 1991? Death, injury, or damage from shelling, death to civilians or civilian injury, or damage to civilian objects?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't have any of those.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would like to -- I'd ask you to --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. I would ask to move this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P111.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If you would next please have a look at tab 12 of your binders. Admiral, in front of you is a document dated 22nd of December, 1991, bearing an endorsement underneath from Colonel -- Colonel-General Pavle Strugar, and it is issued -- excuse me. It concerns dealing with materials referred to as war booty or confiscated materials. Does -- if I can ask you, please, to look through the document. What -- what is -- what prohibitions are brought about, and in particular, in paragraph 5, what types of measures are to be taken against persons who violate the particular subject matter of this order?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order by the command of the 2nd Operational Group dated the 22nd of December. This order was based on an instruction by the Federal Secretary of National Defence. It is about the use of materiel and equipment in the zone of operations. This order is for the organ for civilian administration, and it tasks this specific body with a -- with the management and use of this material and equipment, and the commands of the 9th sector of the 2nd Corps and the republican staff of the Montenegrin Territorial Defence are ordered to cooperate with this civilian administration, but the commands of these units do not have any right to misappropriate this materiel and equipment and hand it over to anyone else. As for those that had been taken over before should be handed over to the assembly centres by no later than the 15th of January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: "And if members of the armed forces and citizens who have unlawfully appropriated materials -- material supplies of any kind," I'm reading from paragraph 5, Admiral, "particularly weapons and ammunition are to be invited in an appropriate and adequate manner to return them and submit them to the assembly centre no later than the 15th of January, 1992, and in this case no criminal proceedings will be instituted against the persons who return the material supplies." Is it your understanding, Admiral, that if they do not return it then criminal proceedings will be instituted?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Admiral.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask to move this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P112.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If you please turn your attention to tab 13 in your binders.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Admiral, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document of my command dated the 22nd of January, 1992, and it bears my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And is this document in some way related to the document we just discussed?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This document is actually an elaboration of the previous order of the commander of the Operative Group, and it has to do with the Vinogradi collection centre which was in my zone. It also has to do how material supplies should be treated within Vinogradi in accordance with the previous orders. That is to say, that things are spelled out in more specific terms and in greater detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you say in accordance with the previous order, are you referring to the order of the 2nd Operational Group?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Admiral, from these two documents, would you -- are you able to indicate or to confirm that misappropriation of war booty was considered a serious offence meriting criminal prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask to move this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is -- that will be Prosecution Exhibit P113.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Admiral, was there a military police unit in the 2nd Operational Group to facilitate or deal with disciplinary measures?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 2nd Operational Group did not have any military police. As far as I know, they only had a reinforced platoon of military police to provide security for the command post and to provide security for various facilities but primarily for its own command. It's only corps and commands that had military police and probably the republican staff of the TO but in Podgorica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Given the -- well, what type of numbers were in this platoon? Can you give numbers of military police to handle the matters in the 2nd Operational Group?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think they had more than 30 to 40 military policemen, and it was only for meeting their own needs of their command post.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Given the indiscipline that you have described in the 2nd Operational Group, were you of the view that there were sufficient military police to deal with those issues?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was the greatest problem, the most pressing problem of all units. That's the way I felt it was. Had I had a battalion or, rather, had I had a regiment of the military police, even that would have been insufficient.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Who could have requested more military police units in the 2OG?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that all subordinate commands tried to resolve that by putting forth a request for additional mobilisation or military police reinforcements that would come from another army. However, this quite simply did not happen. We never succeeded in achieving that. Then I turned company Bar, a Territorial Defence unit, into a military police company, and with a bit of training and having given them police uniforms, we gave them police tasks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Who in the 2nd Operational Group had the authority, at the highest level, who had the authority to seek more military police in circumstances which you indicate merited having more police?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the commander of the 2nd Operative Group.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And that would have been?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Pavle Strugar.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Within the 2nd Operational Group, can you discuss, please, General Strugar's capacity to remove and replace unit commanders in the interests of maintaining discipline?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to the law, the commander of the Second Operational Group was a commander at army level. He could have suspended or replaced a subordinate commander, anybody. That's the kind of authority he had. Any subordinate person he had. He had the right to replace anyone in any superior -- subordinate unit or command. Of course, provided that he reported to his superior command, that is to say the chief of General Staff. If it had to do with higher-ranking officers, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did General Strugar, as the commander of the 2nd Operational Group, exercise this authority to remove where necessary?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he did involving a few examples, but I'm not sure. I heard that as for the commander of a battalion of the Trebinje Brigade, I'm not sure what this was for, and I don't know whether it was for a longer period of time or a shorter period of time, but I think the answer is yes. I don't know of any examples, though. I think it was the commander of the 2nd Battalion or the 1st Battalion of the Trebinje Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not General Strugar removed any officers from the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd or Trebinje Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was at my command post, no. I do not have any such information.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask you to turn your attention, please, to tab 14.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It is, Your Honours, just to remind you, it is already admitted as P45, but it is in your binders.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Admiral, this is a document issued by -- this is a document - excuse me - issued by the General Staff of the SFRY, Lieutenant Blagoje Adzic, and it concerns -- it is dated 29 September 1991. It concerns reporting, transmission of information. Are you familiar with the content of this document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Looking to the first paragraph, if perhaps you might be able to assist with some of the abbreviations where it says "commands of VO, RV." If you would be so good enough to read that first paragraph so that we understood the -- translate the abbreviations. If you could read it out loud, Admiral.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "Number 1, commands of military districts and the air force and the anti-aircraft defence are to submit regular combat reports. Reports are to be submitted on the basis of regular combat reports of the brigades and the corps from three levels down (brigade-regiment, independent battalion-division) for all units and detached formations." And then attachment 40 is explained, these tables according to which the report is being submitted. It says: "Regular combat reports are to be submitted in line with the attachment of the instructions of the work of the commands, attachment number 40, besides the regular combat reports submit extraordinary reports." That is the point.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And, Admiral, it does address the daily submission of reports by 2100 hours, and the compilation or compiling of combat documents in line with instructions. Can you tell us, please, what did this mean for the 2nd Operational Group? How did this translate into reporting for the 2nd Operational Group?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, or subordinate commands of the 2nd Operational Group submit to the 2nd Operational Group its combat reports for its units. The independent battalion was the lowest-ranking unit within the command for which information is provided. That is to say everything that is of relevance to the unit had to be reported. The operations team, the duty team in the staff of the 2nd Operational Group collected these reports from all the units involved and they compiled their own collective report and sent it to the General Staff. That was it, briefly. To the first administration of the General Staff, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you view this then as an indication of, in this instance in the 2nd Operational Group, General Strugar's responsibility as the commander of the Operational Group to keep an efficient flow of information to the highest levels of command as well as from the subordinate levels?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Based on what you have just answered, would that also follow upon inquiry or information about disciplinary matters in subordinate units of the 2nd Operational Group that that information would flow back to General Strugar?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask you, please, to turn to tab -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I just want to check if I've omitted anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Pursuant to your answer about responsibility with indiscipline and the responsibility to act on information coming up, on -- in early November, I believe you may have said the 2nd of November, you had proposed to General Strugar to withdraw the 472nd Brigade because of indiscipline. You indicated that he did not execute your proposal in its entirety and that the 3rd Battalion was left behind. Now, does that conform with acting on the information flow as is described in this order?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that's not quite the way I had put it. Can I explain very briefly now?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Briefly. At the meeting of the 2nd of November, on the basis of requests in terms of how future grouping and use of combat forces should be applied, I suggested that the entire brigade be taken out because it was unnecessary to have a big unit there on the outskirts of Dubrovnik creating problems. Not only because of a lack of discipline. Quite simply, it was not needed. There was no military necessity for it to be there. And General Strugar needed that kind of a unit in the valley of the Neretva River. That was the main reason. That was accepted for the entire brigade on the 2nd of November. That's the only thing I wish to add.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you for your clarification, Admiral. Turning to tab 15, please. Admiral Jokic, this is a directive issued again from Colonel-General Blagoje Adzic dated the 12th of October, and it deals with a number of issues, but in particular I want to turn your attention to the last paragraph of the document. First of all, are you familiar, have you made yourself at any time familiar with the content of this document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether I saw the integral document, the document in its entirety, but it is certain that part of this document was given to the lower commands. Maybe the whole document was read out, but I'd have to read through the whole document. By way of information, I am familiar with all of this. It all looks familiar.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And let me please turn your attention to the last paragraph which states: "All armed units, be they JNA, TO, or volunteer units must act under the single command of the JNA. They should behave and act according to the rules that apply in the army, showing full respect for military discipline, hierarchy, military laws and regulations in all circumstances of life, work, and combat activities. These positions should immediately be communicated to the JNA officers and subsequently in the most suitable manner to soldiers and civilians. This should be illustrated by the most important experience of one's own unit in the past and an outline of the immediate and forthcoming tasks." Does that reflect, Admiral, the importance of General Adzic's order of a single and uniform command within the JNA. Singular - I'm corrected by my colleague - singular and unified command in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask to move to this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P114.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: As a general proposition, Admiral, in the context of singular and unified command, what in your view are the possibilities of a battalion commander initiating combat activity without authority from the relevant command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that could not happen in any combat variant in accordance with our military hierarchy and in accordance with the rules of combat use of our units, I mean the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were you aware, Admiral Jokic, of any politicians in the region where the Dubrovnik operation was being carried out who either interfered, influenced, or worked closely with the 2nd Operational Command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can only know about the mayor of Trebinje, Mr. Vucurevic, Bozidar Vucurevic. There were probably other politicians there, but I did not go very often, so I don't know. He was there often, though, and he was present in the media, in the newspapers, on television all the time. That's how I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Admiral, when I phrased my question to you I used erroneously the phrase 2nd Operational Command. I would correct that to read 2nd Operational Group. Mr. Vucurevic was a mayor, did you indicate, a mayor?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was he affiliated with any political party, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was a member of the SDS, the Serb Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you aware of any views that Mr. Vucurevic held concerning Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had radical views in terms of his attitude towards Dubrovnik and resolving the crisis concerning Dubrovnik. He thought that if Dubrovnik would not accept any demands, the problem would have to be resolved by force. I know that he also had negotiations before. I found this in documents, but it was also carried by the press. He negotiated with the mayor of Dubrovnik, but the announcements he made on radio and TV were well known, that the war against Croats had to be won, and his slogans were very vehement ones and very nationalistic. This influenced junior officers and soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Junior officers and soldiers where, Admiral?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the area of Trebinje. I mean the Dubrovnik operation zone, but specifically, of course, it had to do with Trebinje for the most part. That is where most of the army was concentrated, those troops that took part in the operations that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And those persons would be part of the 2nd Operational Group?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the closest to Kovacevic and Komar who was Chief of Staff of the 472nd Brigade, and he was actually friends with them. Probably with others too, but I know about these two.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you say close to Kovacevic, which Kovacevic are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the commander of the 3rd Battalion of the Trebinje Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You mentioned Komar and Kovacevic. What ethnicity are Komar and Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are Montenegrins from Niksic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you know whether or not Mr. Vucurevic was close with General Strugar?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that. I don't think so. But since he is a very forceful personality and he thought that as a politician he should exercise influence over the military too. He would very often come to the command of the 2nd Operational Group, and he often spend time with the officers and soldiers of the command of the 2nd Operational Group including General Strugar, but I don't think that he could directly influence the reaching of decisions, but indirectly he probably had some influence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was it a usual procedure to frequent the headquarters of the armed forces, for civilians to frequent the headquarters of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, civilians, as far as war is concerned or, rather, a command that is at war, there is a special procedure involved. However, this was the president of a municipality, who beforehand was president of the Serb autonomous province of Herzegovina which was a broader community of all the municipalities of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He was a prominent personality, a prominent figure, a man who always wore camouflage uniform with the insignia of a major as if he were involved in a war, as if he were waging war. So the rules that others were bound by did not apply to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, if you know, what was Mr. Vucurevic's attitude toward the continued existence of Dubrovnik as part of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe his position was that Dubrovnik should have some autonomy, whether as part of Croatia or outside Croatia, I don't know. I'm not familiar with the details. But I assume that he wanted to have Dubrovnik as a town, since together with -- since it had economic links with Trebinje and the hinterland, he wanted some form of autonomy for Dubrovnik, I assume. This is the nebulous idea of some form of autonomy for Dubrovnik as a republic. I think he was in favour of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I ask you to turn to tab 38 in your binders.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Admiral, before you is a letter from Bozidar Vucurevic addressed to -- first of all, dated 7 November 1991, addressed to the chief of headquarters in Belgrade to the military naval command of the Boka Kotorska region, to the 2nd Operative or Operational Group command in Trebinje and to the SFRY Presidency in Belgrade. Would you tell us, please, what this letter says and what impact you perceive it to have been meant to have on the operations in the Dubrovnik area?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This letter is a classic example of his interference with control and command and the way the units were being used. This is a letter that he addressed to the Presidency and to the Chief of the General Staff. He claims that the Croats were targeting our units from the Old Town and from the front end, killing our soldiers. He requests an energetic showdown, as he says, with the Croatian troops. In this letter, he ask that more energetic reserve officers take over the command, as that the JNA was not energetic enough in the way it waged its war, not forceful enough. He even finishes off by saying that something should be changed. He refers to the people who will probably one day judge those who are not doing as -- what they should be doing, in his opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did this type of letter, perhaps even this letter, and the, as you call it, classical example of interference with control and command have an impact on activities or decisions made or revisited in the Dubrovnik theatre by the 2nd Operational Group?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that this was an influential thing. I read the report. I considered it totally unnecessary. I -- I didn't pay attention to it on the day when I read the letter. I thought it was just something very silly. I was, however, mistaken because as early as the 10th with the soldiers in Trebinje, my command had been blocked, laid siege to by the reserve officer and calls were made for my resignation the because of the lack of energy I displayed in the way I waged war on Croatia. The reservists requested that the commander be removed. Therefore, this certainly deserved serious consideration. The negative effect that he had on the morale and on the command. That's as far as his negative influence is concerned. I believe that as far as lower-ranking officers were concerned, Captain Kovacevic and Major Komar, this had very negative influence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'd like to turn your attention now to an area -- excuse me. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I request that this document be submitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P115.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Looking now at the Croatian forces, are you able to give an assessment of the strength of the Croatian forces defending Dubrovnik during the period of 8 October through 6 December 1991? In particular, can you compare them with the forces of the JNA both in terms of numbers and heavy weaponry? Numbers of troops and heavy weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the strength of Croatian paramilitary units, all I can say is that after I arrived at the front on the 8th of October, based on all the intelligence reports and military evaluations that I had, it was our assessment at my command that at the beginning while the operation and the valley of Konavle was under way on the approach road to Dubrovnik, there were between 1.500 and 2.000 such troops, rather, paramilitary units, soldiers. Later when all those elements had withdrawn to Dubrovnik from the surroundings when the town was blocked both from sea and land, above all from land, on the 1st it was also blocked from the sea, we believe that in the town itself following mobilisation and, after all, the groups of the national -- all the groups of the National Guard and the volunteers and the police troops as well as the national defence, that's what they called it, had been assembled, our assessment was that there were between 2.500 and 3.000 soldiers there. They broke through the siege, and they managed to infiltrate a company from the Ston and Metkovic areas into the town. As for their weapons, they had simple automatic weapons, a lot of infantry ammunition, unlimited quantities, I should say. As for the artillery, mostly they had weaker weapons. They had 82-millimetre mortars. They had between 10 and 20 of those. 120-millimetre mortars, we believe between six and ten pieces. We had seized four of those of German make along an approach road to Dubrovnik. They had brought four cannon in from Korcula and four more from Sipan and had those deployed all over Dubrovnik. They had the 20-millimetre two and three barrels, between 10 and 20 pieces. They had rockets. They had the Maljutkas. At the beginning they had several launchers, and they had the Armbrust that they had managed to smuggle into the city. These are German anti-armour rockets. They had two vehicles, one armoured vehicle that they built themselves and another one they somehow fangled together later. As for the ratios in relation to our forces, it's very difficult to provide accurate figures, but are we talking about all units or only about the units in the Dubrovnik zone?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In terms of -- just the Dubrovnik area.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Dubrovnik area, if you put all the units together, I think the result would be between ten and 12.000 in the period where, for example, if you take the beginning of November, the 472nd Brigade was in the blockade together with the battalions and the Territorial Defence. I think there were about 12.000. That was the maximum number, which then dropped to about 3 or 4.000. That's after the entire brigade had pulled out with the exception of the 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Do I understand you correctly then, you're talking about forces of the JNA in the 2nd Operational Group?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, only in the Dubrovnik area. As for the 2nd Operational Group, if you look at that --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, no. Restrict it to Dubrovnik, but you're speaking of the JNA forces?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Admiral.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, Ms. Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If I could just have one more question along this line I think it would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Given the numbers you have shown and what you've described, I believe, as weaker weaponry, did the Croatian forces represent a real threat to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of assessing their combat strength in relation to our forces, we cannot really say that they posed a realistic threat, that they could stop our attack, that they could defeat us or inflict heavy losses on us, certainly not. But in terms of the way they used their resources, they could inflict losses on us by acts of provocation, by ambush, and especially following cease-fires when those acts of provocation were carried out, they would attack us and then they would run. The JNA unit would then strike back and would be blamed for that, and then they would react vehemently to that. So that was the kind of system they used.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was General Strugar aware of the discrepancy in the strength of the two forces, in other words, the forces of the Croatian side and the forces, his forces, General Strugar's forces in the Dubrovnik area?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This would be a convenient time. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have now a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Admiral Jokic, according to information which you may have had while participating in operations around the Dubrovnik area, were there any heavy weapons positions, military installations, or other military activity in the Old Town during the period 7 or 8 October to the end of December 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We suspected especially our lower-ranking officers who were active around Dubrovnik along the approach roads that even in the Old Town there were armed elements that were active as well as some weapons. There was a permanent suspicion with regard to some bits of information that were attained from refugees, but that was no reliable source of information. It was ascertained, however, that there was firing from the town walls and the towers surrounding the Old Town. There was also a vehicle with a weapon mounted on it that occasionally fired from the Old Town. It was moving about in order to avoid being located. Along the approach to the walls itself, there were between four and five 82-millimetre mortars positioned and one 120-millimetre weapon. Later on, there were fewer and fewer of those, especially once we had come very close to the town. There was only that vehicle that I referred to firing from the Old Town itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you learn of the vehicle from first-hand knowledge or from some source after, well after, the incident? After the time of the indictment, rather.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had reliable information on the basis of a testimony by Colonel Marinovic who was the commander of the town's defence. However, our sources kept reporting that there were weapons showing up every now and then, weapons that were being used.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you -- I'm sorry, but when you say "testimony by Colonel Marinovic," what are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean his testimony, the map that he had on which he drew or marked the positions of their guns in Dubrovnik itself and around the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In which case are you referring or to which are you referring, Admiral, when you say "testimony"?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to the first indictment that we had in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you aware or are you able to give the, if any, locations of the 82-millimetre mortars and the 120-millimetre weapon you referred to? Particularly the ones you said close to Old Town, to the town.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was established that throughout the duration of the Dubrovnik operation there were four 82-millimetre mortars in the Bogisic park, which is only 300 metres away from the Pile town gate, and the 120-millimetre mortar was located in the park near the old hospital at about 250 or 300 metres from the walls of the Old Town. This vehicle shuttled between the two gates via the main street, the Stradun, and sometimes they would fire a volley or two.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were you aware at the time of the UNESCO-protected status of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was it known to the troops in the region as well that Dubrovnik, the Old Town, was a protected area?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. You could see UNESCO flags clearly displayed on the walls and turrets.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me just a second. Just taking you back for a moment when you said that the vehicle shuttled between the two gates via the main street, the Stradun, did you know this firsthand or did you hear it from some other source?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew this for sure. We learned this for sure later on, but even during the operations we had information reports that this vehicle was moving up and down the Stradun. And you could see this from an elevation named Zarkovica, which is just above the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So you're indicating that from Zarkovica you could see things on the Stradun?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Is there an unobstructed view from Zarkovica to the Old Town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You could see the Old Town very clearly indeed. The elevation was between 250 and 350 metres high, and the distance between the elevation and the Old Town was between 2 and 3 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Having acknowledged that the Old Town was an UNESCO-protected location, did you ever consider the Old Town as a permissible military target?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We knew that it could never be a military target.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were you aware that civilians were present in the Old Town either living and/or working there?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would like to turn your attention now to tab 16, please. Admiral, can you comment, please. You indicated -- before you proceed, you indicated that you were aware or that the Old Town was never a military target. Was this communicated to all troops in the Dubrovnik area as well?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All the units were duly informed down to the lowest-ranking units.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Admiral. Looking at a document which is issued. It is an order from the Chief of the General Staff of the OS of the armed forces of the SFRY. It is dated 14 October 1991. Are you familiar with the content of this order, Admiral?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, fully.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And looking into the body of the order under the words where it says "Order," particularly at paragraph 3, I turn your attention to the language: "Any attack on cultural property and other protected buildings (churches, historical monuments, medical institutions and suchlike) is strictly forbidden except where units of the JNA come under fire from such buildings. In such cases, the responsible officer shall, prior to opening fire and in a suitable manner, warn the opposite side to cease firing and leave the building." Further in paragraph 4 -- actually, if you continue after that it discusses a policy of reporting and documentation and that: "The military judicial organs should have every violation of the rules of international humanitarian law in the units of operation reported." That is paragraph 4. It is further ordered in paragraph 5 to "circulate this order to all officers and soldiers of the armed forces of the SFRY as well as to all the members of other units engaging in combat in the area of -- areas of JNA operations." Was this order followed in the Dubrovnik area?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were certain aberrations in two specific cases that I know, two serious incidents in November and December, between the 10th and the 12th of November and on the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We will get to those a bit later, Admiral. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask to move this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P116.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask you to please turn your attention to tab 17. This is a document dated 7 November 1991, Admiral, and it is from -- it bears the endorsement of an assistant commander for moral guidance and legal affairs, a major General Vidak Vukovic of the 1st Military District, and I want to call your attention to the theme of it which is a report on the protection of cultural heritage monuments in Yugoslavia. In particular -- First of all, are you familiar generally with the content of this directive?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am. Maybe I did not receive this particular report, but essentially I'm familiar with its content. This speaks about the 1954 Hague Convention and other details that were familiar to the command personnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In the body of the document, Admiral, does it reflect the protections that are to be afforded to cultural property in the event of armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In particular, if you turn to your attention to the second page, which is a carryover from paragraph 2 where it refers to the convention concerning the protection of the world cultural and natural heritage adopted in - sorry - in 1972 and ratified by Yugoslavia in 1975, regulating issues of compiling the world heritage list to include property and areas of global significance in the realm of cultural and natural property to be preserved for future generations. Among UN members, Yugoslavia belongs to the ranks of countries with a large number of places and properties included in the world heritage list, and it cites as the first example, A, the Old City of Dubrovnik. At the bottom, just above the endorsement, above the name, the direction is: "Make certain that the officers and soldiers know of this situation report and the above order of the chief of the Main Staff of the armed forces of the SFRY through the provision of information and direct work in all units especially in the units engaged on the war fronts and in all units sent to the war fronts." You indicated, Admiral, that you were familiar with -- generally the content of this document. Was there --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: -- an extra -- was there an extra effort made to impress and to order the units in the Dubrovnik area under the command and control of the 2nd Operational Group to be mindful of the protected status of cultural institutions, cultural heritage generally, and particularly the Old City of Dubrovnik which was in their area of operation?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The units were informed about this. They were familiarised, and this was obvious in the case of all the units that were near the town of Dubrovnik itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I ask to have the document admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P117.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would you please turn your attention to tab 18. Do you recognise this order, this combat order, Admiral Jokic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a combat order produced by my command, dated the 11th of November 1991, and I signed this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And it is addressed to the 2nd Operational Group, information 9th VPS, and it mentions in its first point that the 472nd Motorised Brigade will continue in its attack in certain areas. It goes on with different aspects of combat issues and -- and I turn your attention to paragraph 6 on the last page of the order. And would you please indicate what is in your order concerning the Old Town of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 6 says that units are forbidden to open fire on the Old Town except in case of lethal fire coming from the area on our units.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Is the term "lethal fire" a term that is used as a -- sort of a general term or a term that comes out of military rhetoric, military parlance?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. If losses in our parts become unacceptable, if there is lethal fire coming in, lethal fire is considered to be the fire that inflicts heavy losses on an units. It was only in this case that they were allowed to fire back. This was an exception that a commander would have been authorised to apply in an extreme situation, in extremis, as the expression goes, but not usually. This would be extremely risky for the unit in question. It would be extremely risky for the unit in question not to be successful in defending itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were any procedures put in place to deal or to respond to lethal fire, for example, initially a warning?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did have a situation like that. Actually, the first situation on the 11th of November, on this very date, when a warning was sent to the Dubrovnik Crisis Staff that civilians, citizens of Dubrovnik, should be removed from the weapons in town that were being used to fire in order to reduce civilian casualties. This was the first and only warning that I can think of, the first and only warning that we sent to the opposite side.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you think of any instances where lethal fire came from the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were several situations where lower-ranking junior commanders were reporting about suffering lethal fire from the town itself but it was never ascertained that it was from the Old Town. The weapons that this lethal fire was coming from was, as a rule, located outside the Old Town or at the front end, the front line of their defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Admiral, I note the date of this order, and can you indicate or can you confirm that it was issued in the midst of an operation by units under your command and control, and of course the command and control of the 2nd Operational Group in the Dubrovnik area?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What was the underlying reason that you saw it necessary to issue this order, particularly with respect to the protected area of Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was meant to protect the Old Town so that it couldn't be fired on except under extremely exceptional circumstances where there was firing from the Old Town that was lethal for the unit. So this was the essence. This was the fundamental meaning. The first time we reached a situation like that was on this date when my units were active, but up to that point we had no combat operations in that direction, at least not as concerns my units. This was merely a form of providing security for the units, for those units that were operating in the immediate surroundings of the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you say "at least not as concerns my units," you mean that there may have been other combat operations under the 2nd Operational Group, but not necessarily by units at the time subordinated to yourself?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Before this date, before I took over as the commander of the Trebinje Brigade, there had been operations the whole time for 26 days when my units were not in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: By this order, Admiral, are you indicating your concern and sensitivity to the need to protect the Old Town of Dubrovnik and the need to be assured that units under your command and control do the same? In combat operations, of course.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's precisely what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask to move this document into evidence, please, to have it admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P118.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before we move on from the document, I wonder, Admiral, if you can clarify for me whether the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- order number 6 on the last page was directed to forces of the 9th Naval Sector or to all forces, that is land forces as well as naval under your command.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. This order pertained to all units under my command, primarily land forces, because in this operation, the naval parts did not actually participate. But of course before and after that, it had to do with them as well. There are other orders pertaining to ships.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Secondly, this order appears to have issued just before midnight on the 11th of November, 1991. Was there any particular reason for the order being issued at the end of that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, probably. Your Honour, this order was issued at 2000 hours. As a rule, orders are issued in the evening for the following day. However, it was necessary to do it this way, in this particular instance because the previously assigned tasks were not carried out. So in order to speed up the operations for this date, the 11th of November, things had to be handled this way. This has to do with bringing in a unit, the 3rd Battalion, which was brought into action for the first time, the 3rd Battalion of the Trebinje Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If you would please turn your attention to document -- I'm sorry, to tab 19. Admiral, before we address the document that I've just referred to, I'd like to ask you as a follow-up to Judge Parker's question, you said in order to speed up the operations for this date, the 11th of November, things had to be handled in -- handled this way. This had to do with bringing in a unit, the 3rd Battalion, which was brought into the action for the first time. Now, was there a particular concern, a safety concern for the Old Town that you are -- that you are linking to the 3rd Battalion of the Trebinje Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the operations between the 8th and the 10th, when the mixed detachment of the Territorial Defence participated, too, we had a weaker unit which had sustained significant losses. I established it only in order to prevent the use of strong artillery, because previously we did not talk about these operations, actually. Before the 11th of November, a unit of the Trebinje Brigade, the 4th battalion had a few provocative actions that they took in that area vis-a-vis the Old Town or, rather, against the hotels outside the Old Town. In order to prevent the repetition of these provocations and the use of strong artillery that this battalion did have, I suggested to the command of the 2nd Operational Group to have this 4th battalion taken out and this mixed detachment of the Territorial Defence was established in its place with weak artillery which could not cause great damage and at a longer distance because the range of their mortars was three kilometres. However, this unit suffered losses. There was a halt in the operation itself, and then a decision was passed in the 2nd Operational Group to bring in the 3rd Battalion of the Trebinje Brigade, and of course the 3rd light brigade which was a unit which was brought into the operations aimed at taking Komolac, which is where the source of Rijeka Dubrovacka is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So the arrival, as I understand you and correct me if I'm wrong, the arrival or the introduction of the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade has some bearing on your issuing this order concerning the protection of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You referred also to the 4th Battalion, and I think you said provocative actions. In what month are you -- do you refer? To what month do you refer about these provocative actions?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was between the 2nd and 4th of November. That's when the Crisis Staff of Dubrovnik protested. I wrote a statement to Admiral Brovet, the deputy Federal Secretary for National Defence about these provocations. Afterwards I suggested to have this battalion withdrawn because with its artillery it could cause certain damage. That was a possibility, but that was not our task.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Not your task because it was not under your command and control at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, what I wanted to say was that the 4th Battalion did not have the task of combat action. On the 25th of October there was a cease-fire, and this cease-fire went on all the way up to the 8th of November officially. In that period of time, between the 2nd of November and the 4th of November, there were these provocations. There was a lack of discipline in that battalion, and sporadic gunfire occurred which did not damage the Old Town, but there was the possibility of incurring further damage in view of the artillery that they had. The 2nd Operational Group had not ordered any action. There was a lull then. There was a cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: On the 2nd of November, however, the 4th Battalion was part of the Trebinje Brigade which was at that time under your command and control?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, we're going back to the document at tab 19. The document is dated 24 October 1991, and it is -- it bears the name commander Major General Pavle Strugar. Are you familiar with this particular document, Admiral, this order?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did receive this order.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you take a look, please, at paragraph 3, and I draw your attention to: "Further to continue to improve the conditions of the accommodation and reliable protection of the people focusing on creation of the overall superiority over the enemy forces and their unconditional surrender. Further to prevent any" -- sorry -- "further to prevent any attacks on the old part of Dubrovnik." Do you know the circumstances or the purpose behind this order of General Strugar's?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The point of this order was the following: That was the first time that the units of the 9th sector were linked up, my units and those of the Trebinje Brigade, which was until then under the direct control of the 2nd Operational Group. Now they needed to take actions together or, rather, the brigade came under the command of the 9th sector. And he calls upon me and the commander of the brigade to come to his command post to prepare for further action.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This was issued on the 24th of October, 1991. Was that during a time of combat operations in the 2nd Operational Group?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Admiral, just to assist us in looking at the Serbo-Croatian version of the document, the one you have, under paragraph 2, I believe there may be, and I want to draw the attention of Your Honours to it, there may be a typographical error not corrected in the English where it says: "The enemy was caused greater losses or bigger losses in manpower," et cetera, et cetera, and 9 VPS forces captured over -- it says 450, but -- I'm sorry. Stricken to 45. Is that correct, Admiral? What does it say in the Serbo-Croatian version of your document is the numbers?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes this is number 45 and 150 is crossed out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, for your attention. And the correction, I would request that it be made in English. I apologise for it not having been caught earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I do turn your attention now, please, or I ask you to turn your attention now to the very last line under "Support." It's a very last line of the document above what would be the sit. It says A and then B: "Artillery. For the further actions, strictly precise the aims in the region of Dubrava and Strincera and north from that line. I strictly forbid the attacks on Dubrovnik." Does that refer to generally the Dubrovnik city?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At first all our orders included a ban on targeting the town of Dubrovnik, and that ban prevailed throughout the operation for the most part. However, when artillery pieces fired from Dubrovnik outside the Old Town, that is, and when this became heavy fire and when we incurred losses, then orders were given to open artillery fire against those targets in order to neutralise them. That is to say, outside the Old Town in order to neutralize those positions from where the shooting came from. And that is why there is repetition of this order strictly forbidding attacks on Dubrovnik. But there was always an explicit ban on targeting the Old Town of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask that this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P119.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Admiral, can you indicate what measures, if any, were taken by the command of the 2nd Operational Group to verify and control the implementation of the orders concerning the protection of the Old Town of do you know?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a few measures at the level of the command of the 2nd Operational Group and at the level of my command. As for the 2nd Operational Group, I know that their chief of artillery often toured artillery units, and he particularly approved firing positions of heavy artillery, the so-called support artillery. Also, I think that there is a particular document where the chief of artillery personally issued tasks to the entire artillery of the 2nd Operational Group that was in action throughout the Dubrovnik zone. This is not customary, but in that document precise orders are given to divisions and to individual batteries in terms of which targets they should engage. Also, there was another measure that artillery observers for support artillery and for artillery for immediate fire should be on elevations from which targets could be viewed. What was forbidden was to open fire at targets that could not be seen, so in such places fire could not be corrected. Those were the three most important measures that are referred to in documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We will now go to tab 20 involving a look at a map. I'm hopeful that we can use the ELMO as much as possible, and if that becomes difficult, I would ask that we use the map board. Before -- while the usher is putting up that or giving you the document to look at, I have a question of you. Considering that there was no necessity for heavy weapons close to the city, why were the weapons left so close? Was that not considered risky?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the way it can be put, absolutely. However, certain restrictions were imposed too. I said a short while ago that as far as heavy artillery is concerned, this support artillery, their firing positions were at distances from which firing positions could be targeted in Dubrovnik. They covered the entirety of Dubrovnik. However, there was also control, but it did not prove to be effective as was seen later. The chief of artillery toured these positions and these artillery units.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would it not, Admiral, have been prudent to have withdrawn the weapons given these concerns?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.
